points.label: South Korea (targeted financial organisations, per CrowdStrike)

impact: Customer personal data, including names, contact details, annual income and loan limits, was exfiltrated from several South Korean financial institutions. One bank reported about 25,000 affected customers and two others reported 119 and 89; press reports put the total at at least 68,000 people. Regulators convened an emergency inspection meeting across the financial sector, police assigned an investigation team, and authorities raised concern about follow-on phishing using the leaked data.
mitigations: South Korea's Financial Services Commission instructed financial companies to inspect all externally accessible IT systems, including non-customer-facing ones, reduce unnecessary information exposure, check for missing or inadequate authentication and access controls, share threat information quickly and submit internal security inspection results.

Korean experts quoted by the press noted that peripheral and supporting systems with weaker authentication were the entry points, and urged banks to strengthen automated, AI-assisted detection and response.
name: ARTEX agentic pentest tool and Claude Code sessions used in data-theft intrusions at South Korean financial institutions

ARTEX AI, Claude agents used in cyberattacks on South Korean banks

summary: From late September to early October 2026 several South Korean financial institutions, including commercial banks, savings banks and other lenders, suffered data breaches. Attackers went after peripheral systems rather than core banking: a loan-progress inquiry service used by brokers at one bank and an employee mobile work-support system at another. Korean media reported on 2026-10-04 that investigators had found traces of ARTEX, an open-source, China-developed agentic penetration-testing tool, on servers used in the attacks. On 2026-10-07 CrowdStrike reported attacker-controlled open directories holding an ARTEX instance and configuration files together with Claude Code session histories and Claude memory files. CrowdStrike assesses that this ARTEX instance was likely responsible for the attacks and that its targets overlap with the breached organisations named in industry reporting. ARTEX ran on DeepSeek v4.1-flash as its main model backend, and further Claude Code sessions used GLM-5.3 and Grok 4.6. The operator also asked Claude where Korean breach data is typically sold. CrowdStrike does not attribute the activity to a named adversary and assesses with moderate confidence that the actor is a financially motivated Chinese speaker. Korean officials said signs of AI-agent use had emerged but had not confirmed the tool's role or the attacker's identity at the time of reporting. Reported victim counts vary between outlets.
